normalize='columns': rows='Robotics', cols=['ChiNext', 'Main', 'STAR', 'All']
normalize='all': rows='All', cols=['ChiNext', 'Main', 'STAR', 'All']
board       ChiNext   Main   STAR    All
tag

Biotech       0.144  0.162  0.000  0.130

  • normalize="index" adds only an All row: the board split across the full sample (58.5% Main). A row-total column would be all ones, so pandas leaves it out.

tag

Cloud         0.163  0.161  0.179

['AI chips', 'Robotics', 'EV battery', 'Cloud', 'Biotech']

400 items -> 837 item-tag rows
[1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
board       ChiNext   Main   STAR
tags                             
AI chips      0.412  0.440  0.464
Biotech       0.485  0.466  0.536
Cloud         0.381  0.410  0.377
EV battery    0.433  0.376  0.333
Robotics      0.402  0.385  0.406

         .value_counts(normalize=True)
         .unstack(fill_value=0))
print(np.allclose(alt, pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, normalize="index")))

True
chi2=15.05  dof=8  p=0.0582

Pass raw counts to chi2_contingency, never a normalized table, because the test depends on sample size. Here p ≈ 0.058. Even with a completely empty STAR × Biotech cell, 400 rows are not quite enough to reject independence at the 5% level. That is a useful reminder not to over-read one striking cell in a percentage table.

FAQ

How do I show crosstab percentages as 0–100 with a % sign?
Multiply by 100 and format at the end, for example (t * 100).round(1).astype(str) + "%", or use t.style.format("{:.1%}") in a notebook. Keep the numeric table for further calculations.

Why don't my row percentages add up to exactly 100?
Rounding. Each cell is rounded separately. Round only for display, or use a largest-remainder method if the displayed numbers must add up.

crosstab or pivot_table?
Same machinery. crosstab takes arrays or Series and has normalize; pivot_table takes a DataFrame and column names and has no normalize, so you divide yourself.

Conclusion

Pick the denominator before you pick the function. normalize="index" answers "how is each row group split?", "columns" answers "what is each column group made of?", and "all" gives joint shares. margins=True adds the matching baseline row or column. Fill NaN keys you want counted, reindex empty categories before normalizing, divide by item counts instead of tag counts for multi-label data, and run significance tests on raw counts.

Stock-to-theme tables are a typical multi-label case: one stock belongs to several concepts, and "share of stocks" and "share of tag assignments" give different answers. Lava's concept stock lookup shows a real version of such a mapping for A-share concept themes.

title: Testing MCP Servers Directly with MCP Inspector
summary:
If you test an AI assistant by trying prompt injection strings for hours, you are testing the wrong boundary.

An LLM is a non-deterministic routing engine. When the model decides to run a task, it emits a structured request to a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server Anthropic's open-source release. That server executes real code on an operating system or database.

To find security vulnerabilities quickly, remove the model entirely. You can interact with the server directly over raw JSON-RPC 2.0 and test its functions like any standard API.

Why prompt injection is the wrong testing tool

Many developers assume their MCP tools will only ever receive clean arguments generated by an AI model. Because the assistant usually behaves politely, developers often forget defensive parameter validation AppSec research on agentic tools.

If you only test tools by arguing with a chatbot interface, you face two hurdles. First, the model's safety guardrails may block your test payloads before they reach the tool. Second, the model might rewrite your strings into valid values.

Real attackers do not need to persuade the model if they can interact with the protocol transport directly. Connecting an evaluation client straight to the server lets you audit the actual application boundaries without token burn or model interference.

Talking directly to JSON-RPC

Anthropic maintains an interactive testing harness called MCP Inspector (@modelcontextprotocol/inspector) that connects directly to servers over standard input and output (stdio) or HTTP transports MCP Inspector documentation.

Instead of opening a web chat interface, you can run the Inspector from your terminal to list all declared capabilities:

# Enumerate declared tools directly without invoking an LLM
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli \
  python3 server.py -- \
  --method tools/list --format json

The target server replies with a list of tools, descriptions, and JSON Schema definitions for every accepted property. The double dash (--) ensures Inspector does not confuse the server's runtime flags with its own options.

Once you have the schema, you can invoke any tool immediately with tools/call. Here is how a tester sends raw payload arguments straight into the target function:

# Send a command injection probe directly to a tool argument
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli \
  python3 server.py -- \
  --method tools/call \
  --tool-name git_log \
  --tool-args-json '{"branch": "; id"}'

Every parameter travels directly to the backend handler. You get immediate, deterministic feedback.

Spotting the dangerous sink

Consider an MCP server designed to let an agent inspect Git repositories. Below is an illustrative vulnerable implementation written in Python using FastMCP:

# Illustrative vulnerable FastMCP server (server.py)
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import subprocess

mcp = FastMCP("DevOps-Helper")

@mcp.tool()
def git_log(branch: str) -> str:
    """Returns commit logs for a git branch."""
    # Dangerous sink: shell=True with concatenated user input
    result = subprocess.run(
        f"git log --oneline {branch}",
        shell=True,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True
    )
    return result.stdout or result.stderr

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Runs the stdio JSON-RPC listening loop
    mcp.run()

The author expected the LLM to pass clean branch names such as main or feature-login. When you send ; id with MCP Inspector, subprocess.run passes the raw string to the system shell, which executes the appended command with the server process privileges.

Reviewing how data reaches sensitive operations is a fundamental skill in software auditing. To see more practical examples of input tracing in modern applications, take a look at the CodeReviewLab guide to tracing untrusted input to dangerous sinks.

Securing the tool handler

Fixing this flaw requires two defences. First, avoid running system commands through a shell interpreter. Second, enforce a strict allowlist on caller arguments before they reach any operating system API.

Here is an illustrative remediated version of the tool:

# Illustrative secure FastMCP server (server.py)
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import subprocess
import re

mcp = FastMCP("DevOps-Helper")
BRANCH_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_\-\.\/]+$")

@mcp.tool()
def git_log(branch: str) -> str:
    """Returns commit logs for a git branch."""
    # Reject unexpected characters and leading command flags
    if not BRANCH_PATTERN.match(branch) or branch.startswith("-"):
        raise ValueError("Invalid branch name format.")

    # Safe sink: direct array arguments with shell=False
    result = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "log", "--oneline", "--", branch],
        shell=False,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=10,
        check=False
    )
    return result.stdout or result.stderr

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

This pattern disables shell meta-character parsing entirely. Passing -- ensures Git does not treat a branch name starting with a dash as an option flag.

Parameter validation inside the tool protects the underlying host, but it does not prevent an LLM from misinterpreting poisoned data returned by external tools. For a deeper breakdown of system boundaries in agent environments, check out the CodeReviewLab guide to MCP security.

When the server attacks your inspector

There is an important catch when testing third-party or untrusted MCP servers. Your testing harness is also software, and it can be vulnerable.

Early releases of @modelcontextprotocol/inspector had serious flaws. Versions prior to 0.14.1 ran an unauthenticated local Node proxy binding to 0.0.0.0 on port 6277 CVE-2025-49596 security advisory. This allowed malicious websites to execute commands locally through cross-origin requests or DNS rebinding.

Later, stored cross-site scripting in the OAuth debugging interface allowed rogue servers to trigger local command execution Miggo Security's writeup on CVE-2025-58444. Even in the modern v2 series, versions before 2.12.0 could be exploited by a malicious server returning forged OAuth URLs that injected PowerShell commands on Windows systems Pillar Security advisory for CVE-2026-119025.

When assessing an untrusted server, keep these precautions in mind:

  1. Always update @modelcontextprotocol/inspector to version 2.12.0 or later before connecting to untrusted hosts.
  2. Never start the Inspector with authentication disabled using flags such as DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH=true.
  3. Run your assessment inside an isolated container or virtual machine rather than directly on your primary workstation.

Review checks for MCP servers

When auditing or building an MCP server, verify these core areas:

  • Input boundaries: Validate every argument against a strict schema. Reject undeclared properties and unexpected types.
  • Process isolation: Never pass tool arguments into shell=True or unescaped terminal strings. Pass isolated argument lists directly to executables.
  • Transport authentication: If using remote Streamable HTTP transports, ensure the server authenticates callers and checks OAuth token scopes against expected resources.
  • Description integrity: Audit tool descriptions returned by tools/list to ensure external sources have not embedded prompt injection payloads inside metadata.

Testing tools directly gives you fast, repeatable results without relying on model luck. If you want to practise tracing untrusted inputs across different languages and frameworks, visit CodeReviewLab to work through hands-on review challenges.

title: Recording a YouTube live stream with yt-dlp (the flags that actually matter)
summary:
If you've tried to grab a YouTube live stream with yt-dlp and ended up with half a broadcast or just an error, the thing to know is that a live stream isn't a finished file - it's an ongoing feed, and a couple of flags decide what you actually get.

Here's what I've landed on.

Just record from now 

yt-dlp "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIDEO_ID"

Point it at a stream that's live and it records from the current moment until the broadcast ends (or you ctrl-c). No special flag needed for a basic capture - the live URL is the same /watch?v= one as any other video.

Catch it from the start 

yt-dlp --live-from-start "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIDEO_ID"

By default yt-dlp joins where the stream currently is, so anything broadcast before you ran the command is gone. --live-from-start rewinds to the beginning. It can pull a lot of data for a long stream and it's slower because it has to walk every fragment, but it's the only way to get the opening.

Wait for a stream that hasn't started yet 

yt-dlp --wait-for-video 30-600 --live-from-start "URL"

A plain command just errors out if the stream isn't live yet. --wait-for-video MIN-MAX keeps re-checking (those are the min/max seconds between checks) and starts the moment it goes live. Handy to leave running ahead of a scheduled premiere.

Keep a playable file if the capture drops 

yt-dlp --live-from-start --hls-use-mpegts -N 4 "URL"

A capture can run for hours, so assume it'll get interrupted. --hls-use-mpegts writes to an MPEG-TS container that stays playable even if the process dies mid-stream, so you keep what you recorded instead of a corrupt file. -N 4 grabs a few fragments at once to keep up with a high-bitrate stream. When it ends cleanly you can --remux-video mp4 if you need something more portable.

The honest caveats

  • A live stream can't be retried. For a normal video a failed fragment is just re-requested. In a live capture there's no going back in time, so if the connection drops for a stretch, that part of the broadcast is simply gone.
  • Some live formats need a PO token now. Missing it shows up as missing formats or a capture that stops after a short while.
  • Keep yt-dlp updated. Player changes break live extraction faster than they break normal downloads - run yt-dlp -U before a scheduled capture, not during one.

Why it's worse on a server

If you're running this from a VPS or a CI runner, you've got two problems stacked. YouTube throttles and blocks datacenter IPs harder than home connections, so a server capture is more likely to hit a mid-stream block. And because a live stream can't be replayed, that block turns into a permanent gap instead of a retry. The free fix is to run captures from a clean residential IP, keep yt-dlp current, and use --live-from-start --hls-use-mpegts so an interruption still leaves a usable partial file.

fwiw I run a hosted API for exactly this "works on my laptop, dies on the server" problem (I built importly.io - you POST a URL and get the file or transcript back from infra that isn't blocked), so if you're capturing from a server and don't want to babysit IPs it might save you some time. For a one-off from your own machine though, the flags above are all you need.

Full writeup with the related guides: https://ytdlp.org/guides/yt-dlp-download-youtube-live

title: The last Python 3.9 you can install from python.org is from 2022
summary:
I have one rule for this kind of post: open the primary source myself before writing a word. This one started because "we're already on the last 3.9" is a sentence I would have said out loud without checking, and I didn't want to be the person who said it.

The claim, as it usually gets written

Python 3.9 reached end of life on 2025-10-31. The last release is 3.9.25. So if you have to stay on 3.9 a little longer, install 3.9.25.

Correct about the dates. Wrong about what you can install.

What the primary sources actually say

PEP 596, Python 3.9 Release Schedule. I read the source RST, not a summary of it:

- 3.9.13 final: Tuesday, 2022-05-17
  (Final regular bugfix release with binary installers)

and, for everything after that:

Source-only security fix releases
Provided irregularly on an "as-needed" basis until October 2025.

Then I checked what python.org actually hands you. Its release API lists the files per release. For 3.9.25 there are two, and both are source tarballs (.tgz, .tar.xz). For 3.9.13 there are nine, including the Windows installer and the embeddable package.

Which means two sentences, both true

  • latest 3.9 release: 3.9.25, 2025-10-31, source only
  • latest 3.9 python.org gives you a ready-made installer for: 3.9.13, 2022-05-17

Twelve source-only security releases sit between them. A machine that was installed back then and never rebuilt from source has all twelve outstanding, and no amount of writing "latest" in a runbook fixes that.

Where the claim does hold

Docker's official images still ship it. The Hub lists 3.9.25-slim, 3.9.25-slim-trixie, 3.9.25-alpine3.22, all built 2025-11-01, because the image maintainers compile from source. So "just use the container" is fine and current.

That narrows it, it doesn't kill it. The failure is any automation that expects an installer from python.org: an Ansible role, a CI cache warmed years ago, a pyenv pin that assumes a binary, a Windows agent image.

The one word that cost the check

Install carries a builder. A version number doesn't.

3.9.25 on python.org is two tarballs. 3.9.25 on Docker Hub is a built image. 3.9.25 in a distro package is whatever the distro patched, possibly with the version string left alone. Three different things, one number, and the number is the part everyone quotes.

So when a version shows up in an upgrade ticket, the question isn't "is that the latest". It's what the number is attached to: whose build, from when, with which security window behind it. If the answer is "the latest one", the sentence is about a date, not about a binary you can run.

Sources, all reopened before writing

  • PEP 596 source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/peps/main/peps/pep-0596.rst
  • python.org release API, file list: ?release=1075 (3.9.25, 2 files) and ?release=717 (3.9.13, 9 files) at https://www.python.org/api/v2/downloads/release_file/
  • Docker Hub tags for library/python filtered to 3.9

title: Un jeu de données ouvert sur les salons de jardin, en CSV et en JSON
summary:
Schéma, licence, conventions de calcul et requêtes de contrôle pour le fichier du 17 novembre 2026.

Le catalogue du comparateur Quel salon de jardin est publié sous licence CC BY 4.0, sous deux formes : un CSV et un JSON. Le fichier daté du 17 novembre 2026 contient 364 lignes, une par modèle publié et indexé sur le site. Il ne contient ni photo ni lien vers les marchands.

Formats et mise à jour

  • CSV : UTF-8 avec BOM, séparateur virgule. Le BOM impose encoding="utf-8-sig" en Python, sinon la première colonne s'appelle ﻿slug.
  • JSON : une enveloppe de métadonnées autour des lignes.
  • Les deux fichiers sont régénérés après chaque relevé de prix. Leur date_releve est le jour du relevé le plus récent, pas la date de collecte de chaque ligne.

L'enveloppe JSON comporte les clés nom, producteur, source, licence, licence_url, date_releve, nb_lignes, colonnes (nom et description de chaque colonne) et lignes.

Schéma

Identification et classement :

  • slug, url_fiche, nom, marque, type

Caractéristiques :

  • matiere_structure, places, couleurs
  • largeur_cm, profondeur_cm, hauteur_assise_cm, poids_kg
  • longueur_table_cm, largeur_table_cm, diametre_table_cm : ensembles repas ou salons de balcon, quand la valeur est publiée
  • garantie_mois

Prix et offres :

  • prix_min_eur, prix_max_eur, prix_par_place_eur, nb_offres, marchands, date_releve

Conventions :

  • cellule vide = valeur non publiée pour ce modèle (pas zéro) ;
  • prix en euros TTC, hors livraison ;
  • prix_par_place_eur = prix_min_eur / places, arrondi au centime ;
  • date_releve au format AAAA-MM-JJ, heure de Paris ;
  • marchands : noms séparés par un point-virgule, sans URL.

Taux de remplissage

Sur les 364 lignes :

Champ Lignes renseignées
matiere_structure 356
prix_min_eur 337
places 290
hauteur_assise_cm 164
poids_kg 77
largeur_cm et profondeur_cm 44
longueur_table_cm et largeur_table_cm 37
diametre_table_cm 7

Les 44 lignes avec une emprise au sol complète comptent 29 bains de soleil, 10 salons de jardin bas, 3 salons d'angle et 2 ensembles repas. Un agrégat de dimensions calculé là-dessus décrirait surtout des bains de soleil.

Requêtes de contrôle

Compter les lignes et les types, en Python standard :

import csv
from collections import Counter

with open("salons-de-jardin.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

len(rows)  # 364
Counter(r["type"] for r in rows)
# Salon de jardin bas 212, Ensemble repas de jardin 64,
# Bain de soleil 36, Salon de jardin d'angle 26,
# Salon de jardin pour balcon 26

Vérifier la date et la taille du fichier JSON avant de l'exploiter :

jq '{date_releve, nb_lignes}' salons-de-jardin.json
# {"date_releve": "2026-11-17", "nb_lignes": 364}

Si nb_lignes ou date_releve ne correspondent plus, le fichier a été régénéré depuis : les chiffres de cet article sont alors à reprendre.

Reproduire les médianes du site

Le site agrège prix_min_eur, c'est-à-dire le prix le plus bas relevé pour chaque modèle, et ne publie une médiane que pour les groupes d'au moins trois modèles. Il s'agit d'une médiane basse : sur la liste triée, la valeur d'indice floor(0.5 * (n - 1)). Sur un groupe de taille paire, statistics.median ou pandas.Series.median(), qui moyennent les deux valeurs centrales, peuvent donner un autre résultat.

Deux périmètres coexistent :

  • médiane d'ensemble « salon de jardin » : bains de soleil exclus, soit 566,99 € sur 301 modèles ;
  • tableaux par matière et par places : tous les modèles avec un prix, bains de soleil inclus.

Quelques valeurs au 17 novembre 2026 :

Groupe Modèles avec prix Médiane
Aluminium 127 1 406 €
Résine tressée 127 499,90 €
Acier 38 234,71 €
« 2 places » 61 203,99 €
« 10 places et plus » 25 799,99 €

Les libellés de places sont des tranches et non des effectifs exacts : « 2 places » couvre 1 à 2, « 4 places » 3 à 4, « 6 places » 5 à 6, « 8 places » 7 à 9, « 10 places et plus » 10 et au-delà. Pour regrouper la colonne places comme le site, il faut appliquer ces bornes.

Ces médianes rapprochent des modèles différents à une date donnée. Elles ne mesurent pas l'effet propre d'une matière, d'une marque ou d'une taille.

Licence, citation et copies

CC BY 4.0 : réutilisation libre, y compris commerciale, avec attribution à Quel salon de jardin (Bastien Hugon EI). Forme de citation demandée :

Quel salon de jardin (Bastien Hugon EI), « Prix et dimensions des salons de jardin vendus en ligne en France », relevé du 17 novembre 2026, https://quel-salon-de-jardin.fr/donnees, licence CC BY 4.0.

Des copies existent sur data.gouv.fr, Hugging Face, Kaggle, Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24176950) et dans le dépôt salons-de-jardin-donnees sur GitHub. Ces copies peuvent dater d'un relevé antérieur ; la version à jour des fichiers et de leur description se trouve sur la page de données du site.
